h1: Launching a beer brand in a new market
title: Launching a Beer Brand in a New Market | Craft Beer School
desc: How to launch a beer brand in a new market: research the shelf, check the name and trademark, adapt labels and pack, choose partners and run a small test.
teaser: A beer that sells at home may not sell abroad. Check the name, the rules, the price and the climate before you ship.
standfirst: Entering a new market multiplies the work: new rules, new language, new distributors, new habits. This guide sets the order that keeps mistakes cheap.
sections: Study the shelf and the menu

Spend time where the beer will be sold: bars, shops, restaurants, supermarkets. Note styles, pack sizes, prices, brand looks and who is missing. Ask what customers drink with the local food. A gap in the market exists only if people want to buy something to fill it.

Talk to bartenders, shop buyers and ordinary drinkers. Ask what they buy, what they would try and what puts them off. Spend time on price: a beer priced well above its neighbours needs a clear reason. One priced below may look cheap.

Check how much beer is sold through bars compared with shops, since that decides your pack, your partners and your marketing.

A name can mean something rude, silly or confusing in another language. Check pronunciation and meaning with local speakers. Then search trademarks in the market, since a name free at home may be taken there. See naming a beer for more than one language and protecting a beer name in more than one country.

Take legal advice before you print anything.

Look at the visual side as well. Colours carry meanings that differ between cultures. Some imagery is unwelcome or restricted. A local designer or reviewer can spot problems before they cost you a print run.

Do not forget the web. A domain, social handles and app store names may be taken even when the trademark is free. Check them before you commit to a name.

Trademark rights are mostly national or regional, so registering in one country does not protect you in the next. Ask an adviser which markets to file in first. File before you announce.

Each market sets its own rules for alcohol imports, labels, strength, pack size and advertising. Some require an importer licence, others a local distributor. Check them early and write down what you learn. See what a beer label must show.

Where alcohol is restricted, local law comes first.

Marketing rules are separate from label rules. Many markets limit where and how alcohol can be advertised, who can appear in adverts and what claims can be made. Social media is covered in many of them. Never target young people. Keep the tone responsible.

Beer travels and waits. Heat shortens shelf life. Light and oxygen make it worse. Choose a package that suits the climate and the cold chain. See can or bottle for hot markets. Print dates clearly and agree who checks stock age.

Think about the whole journey from your brewery to the glass. Ports, warehouses, trucks and shop shelves all add heat and time. Ask the distributor how beer is stored and for how long. Agree a shelf-life rule so old stock is withdrawn.

Most brands enter a market through an importer or distributor. Ask for references, check what other brands they carry and how they store beer. Agree who sets price, who pays for promotion and how stock returns work. Put terms in a written agreement, with legal advice.

Be clear about who owns the brand in the market. The agreement should say whether the partner has exclusive rights, for how long and what happens if sales fall short. Take legal advice before you sign.

Start with one city, a few venues and a small order. Track sales, feedback and shelf life. Adjust the pack, price or range before you scale. Build the brand story from what customers say, not from what you wish they said.

A brand strategy keeps the choices consistent: who the beer is for, what it stands for and how it looks and sounds in each market.

Set a review point, such as three or six months, with simple measures: cases sold, venues won, repeat orders and feedback. Decide in advance what result means grow, adjust or stop.

Keep a note of what you learn in each market. The second launch should be quicker and cheaper than the first. See starting a beer brand with contract brewing if you want to test a market without a local brewery.
faqs: Should I change my brand for a new market?
Sometimes. Keep what makes it recognisable and change names, labels or flavours that clash with local language or law.
Do I need a local partner?
Often, because of import rules and distribution. The right partner knows the trade and the regulations.
How much beer should I ship first?
A small amount that tests the market without a large loss if it fails. Match volume to how fast the beer can sell while fresh.
